walkthroughs.body_html:
Electric Circuits — a core area of A-Level Physics.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Electric Circuits brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Electric Circuits.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: If the separation between two point charges is halved, the force becomes:
options: Halved
Doubled
Quartered
Quadrupled

mcqs.q: The electric field between parallel plates 5.0 mm apart with a p.d. of 200 V is:
options: 1 kV m⁻¹
40 kV m⁻¹
100 V m⁻¹

mcqs.q: In which direction does an electric field point near a positive charge?
options: Radially outwards — the field is defined by the force on a positive test charge, which is repelled.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
Radially inwards because positive attracts negative.

mcqs.q: What happens to the total resistance when you add another resistor in parallel?
options: Adding any resistor always increases the total resistance.
Total resistance decreases — there are more paths for current to flow.
Adding a parallel resistor doubles the voltage available.
There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.

mcqs.q: If the distance between two masses doubles, what happens to the gravitational force between them?
options: There is no field around a positive charge unless another charge is present.
It halves — gravitational force is inversely proportional to distance.
It quarters — gravitational force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
It doubles — more distance means more space for gravity to act through.
